source.title: Into the Rabbit Hull: From Task-Relevant Concepts in DINO to Minkowski Geometry
source.authors: Thomas Fel; Bin-Xun Wang; Michael A. Lepori; Matthew Kowal; Andrew Lee; Randall Balestriero; Sonia Joseph; E. Lubana; Talia Konkle; Demba E. Ba; Martin Wattenberg

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study discusses neuron-aligned versus distributed representations, but does not test the claim’s neuron-pole audit or any of its specified versions.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes SAE dictionary concepts in DINOv2-B, not the share of neuron poles with one or more named jobs. Its Hoyer-score result concerns whether dictionary atoms align with individual units; it does not evaluate neuron explanations on held-out activations, score explanations by simulated firing, or compare models, architectures, or tools for interpretability share.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes SAE dictionary atoms in DINOv2-B (task recruitment, geometry, Hoyer sparsity, Minkowski hypothesis). It never audits individual neurons' jobs, scores neuron explanations, examines InceptionV1 polysemantic neurons, compares tools or architectures for neuron interpretability share, or builds neuron-based attribution graphs. It repeats the standard view that neurons are polysemantic as background, which is discussion rather than a test of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that DINOv2-B SAE concepts show task specialization and are distributed rather than neuron-aligned. The dictionary departs from near-orthogonal sparse coding: it is more coherent than a Grassmannian frame and anisotropic, contains antipodal pairs and dense positional features, and token clouds stay locally connected after position is removed. They propose the Minkowski Representation Hypothesis as a working hypothesis, supported by theory and preliminary, model-specific evidence, and explicitly do not claim to contradict the Linear Representation Hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns and analyzes a vision-model SAE dictionary and representation geometry; it does not generate or test natural-language neuron explanations or evaluate them on held-out activations.

fits_no_version.finding: DINOv2-B SAE atoms have Hoyer scores far below the one-hot bound and are only slightly sparser than random Gaussian vectors, so learned concepts are distributed across units.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In DINOv2-B, SAE-derived concept directions are distributed across many units rather than aligned with individual neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE concepts whose activation location dissociates from their causal source ('Elsewhere' concepts) mean that activation heatmaps can mislead about what a concept encodes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For DINOv2 SAE concepts, where a concept fires can differ from the image region that causally drives it.

record.problems: The evidence relevant to neuron alignment is a dictionary-level Hoyer-score analysis, not a direct audit of neuron explanations. The study itself describes its geometric evidence as preliminary and model-specific.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted: task specialization, positional information, token geometry, and convex-geometric analyses do not measure neuron-pole job counts or any other version’s specified outcome.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares (about 90% one job, 7% two jobs, 2–4% unexplained).
Neuron interpretability shares in other language models, dense and MoE, at any scale.
Reinterpretation of InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons as pose detectors (recursive generalization vs superposition).
Whether the interpretable-neuron share rises with better tools or modern architectures.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.

Whether explanations built from activating examples predict firing elsewhere. The 'Elsewhere' concepts concern SAE concepts and the localization-vs-causation gap, not neuron explanations on held-out data.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Vision SAE study, not a neuron audit. Its reliance on the view that neurons are polysemantic is cited background, not a new measurement on neurons. The 'Elsewhere' finding resembles V6 in spirit, but it concerns SAE concept heatmaps versus RISE causal maps, not neuron explanations tested on held-out text.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit shares and neuron-pole job counts.
Comparisons across language models, dense and MoE models, or parameter scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car and pose explanations, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Interpretability shares across tools, architectures, or InceptionV1-sized models.
Attribution graphs built from a model’s own neurons and comparisons with replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Automated explanation scoring by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: DINOv2-B
rows.operation_detail: Measured Hoyer sparsity scores of learned SAE dictionary atoms as an indicator of alignment with individual units.
rows.measure: Hoyer sparsity scores of dictionary atoms
rows.baseline: One-hot, neuron-aligned limit 1.0; Gaussian-vector reference 1 − 2/π ≈ 0.202; random-vector baseline also shown.
rows.value: Scores remain below the one-hot bound; compared with random baselines, SAE atoms are slightly sparser but remain broadly distributed.
rows.note: This measures SAE dictionary atoms, not the proportion of neuron poles with interpretable jobs.
rows.check: The row measures the Hoyer sparsity of SAE dictionary atoms relative to the neuron basis. It does not measure what share of neurons have one interpretable job, so it cannot bear on any version. The state 'observed' has no version-level meaning here. The value is correctly read: atoms sit below the one-hot bound and are slightly sparser than the Gaussian baseline of about 0.202.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
